profile.summary: Vladimir Breygin is a senior transformation and product executive with roughly 15 years spanning capital markets, investment banking, and FinTech, including a Global Head of Risk & Regulatory role at Bank of America Merrill Lynch and a CIO/COO mandate at Sberbank CIB where he managed a $50M P&L. His current advisory and consulting practice (ESP) focuses on enterprise digital transformation rather than running a large internal IT operations function, and his CV skews heavily toward product strategy and transformation leadership rather than steady-state IT operations management at scale.

gaps.detail: No role on the CV states a direct or total headcount. The largest budget figure is $50M at Sberbank CIB. The RBC Capital Markets role requires demonstrated ownership of a 400-person team and $100M opex. Per the scale-leadership threshold rule, the CV cannot substantiate managers-of-managers experience at this scope, and the leadership dimension score is capped at 6/10 as a result.
gaps.headline: No evidenced large-team headcount or budget authority
gaps.role_mismatch: The role's 9/10 leadership weight demands evidenced management of a senior technology organisation at bulge-bracket or near-equivalent scale — this candidate cannot demonstrate that bar from available CV data.

gaps.detail: Since 2017 Breygin has operated exclusively as an external consultant and practice director at ESP. The transition from advising clients on digital transformation to owning the P&L, headcount, and 24/7 operational risk of a large CIB IT function is a material step-change. There is no recent evidence of managing incident response, infrastructure SLAs, or run-the-bank obligations.
gaps.headline: Seven years out of in-seat operational leadership
gaps.role_mismatch: The Head of IT Operations role requires an operator mindset with live accountability for system uptime and operational resilience — the CV evidences an advisory and product-design posture for the most recent seven years.

gaps.detail: The CV references cloud, big data, and AI generically but names no specific post-trade or capital markets infrastructure platforms (Murex, Calypso, Broadridge, FIS GMI). For a Head of IT Operations at a global CIB, platform ownership — not consultative exposure — is a baseline expectation. The technical dimension score of 5/10 reflects this gap directly.
gaps.headline: No named post-trade platform or infrastructure ownership
gaps.role_mismatch: With a technical weight of 8/10, the absence of named infrastructure and post-trade platform ownership against which operational accountability can be assessed is a critical evidential gap.

strengths.detail: Breygin held a Global Head of Risk & Regulatory title at Bank of America Merrill Lynch and a dual CIO/COO seat at Sberbank CIB, giving him front-to-back CIB exposure across risk, regulatory, and trading technology. This is not generic financial services; the roles sit inside investment banking divisions with direct trading-desk adjacency.
strengths.signal: He will navigate RBC Capital Markets stakeholders — trading desks, risk officers, and compliance — with credibility that a candidate from a non-CIB background would lack.
strengths.headline: Tier-1 capital markets domain pedigree

strengths.detail: The Sberbank CIB FinTech trading platform was built from inception to full production under his leadership, with reported 40% revenue increase and 50% client acquisition growth attributed to the programme. At BofA Merrill Lynch he led a global regulatory and risk programme overhaul. These are multi-phase, cross-functional deliveries, not advisory engagements.
strengths.signal: He can lead a live modernisation mandate at RBC Capital Markets with the pattern-recognition of someone who has shipped complex CIB technology programmes before, not just designed them.
strengths.headline: End-to-end transformation programme delivery

strengths.detail: His BofA Merrill Lynch tenure (2012–2014) centred on global regulatory and risk programme delivery at a point when post-crisis regulatory pressure was at its peak — Dodd-Frank, Basel III, and EMIR were all in simultaneous flight. The CV does not name specific frameworks but the institutional context and title are credible signals of deep regime exposure.
strengths.signal: He is unlikely to be surprised by the regulatory overhead of a Head of IT Operations role at RBC Capital Markets and should be able to engage substantively with compliance and audit functions.
strengths.headline: Regulatory and risk technology programme ownership

strengths.detail: Breygin drove Agile transformation at Sberbank CIB across a fintech build, and at ESP has directed the full lifecycle of 15+ enterprise solutions concurrently. His self-identification as a CPO-archetype means he applies product-management discipline — roadmaps, OKRs, delivery cadences — to large, complex IT environments.
strengths.signal: This predicts strong execution rigour and the ability to impose delivery structure on the IT operations function during a modernisation phase.
strengths.headline: Agile and product lifecycle leadership at scale

comparison.positioning: No other candidates have been provided in this slate, so relative positioning cannot be assessed. Breygin is evaluated on an absolute basis only.

positioning.opener: Vladimir Breygin brings a rare combination of front-to-back CIB domain credibility — Global Head of Risk & Regulatory at Bank of America Merrill Lynch, CIO/COO at Sberbank CIB with a $50M P&L — and a substantive track record of delivering complex transformation programmes inside tier-1 investment banking environments.
talking_points: His BofA Merrill Lynch and Sberbank CIB tenures give him the capital markets fluency to engage immediately with trading-desk stakeholders and risk officers — this is not a candidate who needs a domain induction.
He has shipped a FinTech trading platform from inception to production and led a global regulatory programme overhaul, which maps directly to the modernisation mandate inside this role.

If the client is willing to explore a structured transition plan — for example, pairing him with a strong COO or Head of Infrastructure in the first 12 months — the domain and transformation credentials could justify the operator-to-advisor reintegration risk.
positioning.objection_handling: The most likely client objection is that he has not run a 400-person IT operations function and has been consulting for seven years — the honest response is to acknowledge both gaps directly and position this as a transformation-first hire that requires a complementary operational deputy, rather than a steady-state operations incumbent.

final_verdict.narrative: Against the two highest-weighted dimensions — domain (10) and leadership (9) — Breygin scores 7 and 6 respectively, and the alignment test returns red on the single most important operational must-have: evidenced ownership of a large IT function at tier-1 scale. The weighted profile (approximate weighted score of 6.33 across all five dimensions, dragged down by the leadership and technical gaps) places him at the lower end of tier_3 — a stretch fit that is hard to position credibly given the seven-year consulting gap and the absence of any headcount or infrastructure-scale data. This is not an off-profile candidate on domain, but it is an off-mandate candidate on operational scope.

scoring_table.commentary: Breygin's tech exposure spans cloud, big data, AI, and SaaS at a conceptual level through his ESP advisory practice, but the CV provides no evidence of hands-on IT infrastructure ownership, SRE, or named post-trade platforms (Murex, Calypso, Broadridge). For a Head of IT Operations role carrying an 8/10 technical weight, the absence of infrastructure depth and specific system ownership is a material deficit.

Genuine capital markets and CIB domain credentials: Global Head of Risk & Regulatory at Bank of America Merrill Lynch (2012–2014) and CIO/COO at Sberbank CIB managing a $50M P&L (2014–2017). Asset class and desk-level specificity are not quoted in the CV, and post-2017 domain exposure has been consultative rather than operational inside a tier-1 bank.

The CV references board-level engagement and directorial titles but provides no direct headcount, managers-of-managers structure, or budget authority approaching the 400-person team and $100M opex mandate required. Per scale-leadership threshold rules, without evidenced managers-of-managers experience this dimension cannot exceed 6/10 for a Head-of role at this scope.

Bank of America Merrill Lynch Global Head of Risk & Regulatory role (2012–2014) implies FCA/PRA and likely Dodd-Frank exposure, and Sberbank CIB suggests awareness of CIB regulatory frameworks. However, no specific regulatory regime (SMCR, Basel III/IV, MiFID II, Reg SCI) is named in the CV, capping this score at 6/10 per the regulatory validator rule.

Three substantive programmes are evidenced: a FinTech trading platform built from inception to production at Sberbank CIB, a global regulatory and risk overhaul at BofA Merrill Lynch, and enterprise-wide digital transformation at ESP. The Sberbank programme is the closest to a named, scoped transformation artefact ($50M P&L, Agile adoption), but budget, duration, and decommission outcomes are not quoted for the others, limiting confidence.

alignment_test.answer: The CV does not provide team size for any role. The largest budget figure cited is a $50M P&L at Sberbank CIB, which is materially below the $100M opex threshold, and Sberbank CIB, while a substantial CIB, is not a tier-1 global bulge-bracket institution. Post-2017 he has operated as an external consultant, not an in-seat operator of a large IT function. Evidence for this specific must-have is absent.
alignment_test.question: Can this candidate evidence direct ownership — headcount, budget, and P&L — of a 300-plus person IT operations function inside a tier-1 investment bank or equivalent regulated institution?
alignment_test.justification: The CV provides no headcount data for any role and the largest budget evidenced ($50M at Sberbank CIB) falls short of the $100M threshold, with the consulting-to-operator gap compounding the absence — this is a red against the role's single most critical operational must-have.

profile_summary.executive_summary: Vladimir Breygin is a capital markets transformation executive with 15 years spanning Bank of America Merrill Lynch, Sberbank CIB, and a seven-year advisory practice at ESP, where he has directed product strategy and enterprise digital programmes. His domain credentials are genuine but his operational mode since 2017 has been external consulting, not running a large-scale internal IT operations function — the implicit ask is whether a consulting-to-operator transition at this scope (400 people, $100M opex) is credible. Against the two highest-weighted dimensions — domain (10) and leadership (9) — he meets the domain bar only partially and falls short on evidenced leadership scale.

evaluation.recommendation_rationale: Tier_3 classification driven by a red alignment-test result on the leadership scale must-have and a seven-year consulting gap means the candidate cannot be credibly presented as a primary or secondary shortlist candidate for a Head of IT Operations role with a 400-person team and $100M opex mandate.

Zero headcount data on CV; leadership scale at $100M opex cannot be substantiated.

role_pattern.evidence: The career arc moves from CIO/COO at boutique capital markets firms (GBSG, Vander Mollen, UCSG, 2010–2012) to Global Head of Risk & Regulatory at BofA Merrill Lynch, then CIO/COO at Sberbank CIB with P&L ownership, then Global Practice Director at ESP — each move targets a larger title or broader mandate, consistent with a climber pattern.

risk_tolerance.evidence: He moved from a bulge-bracket advisory role at BofA Merrill Lynch to building a FinTech trading platform from scratch at Sberbank CIB (a non-tier-1 institution), then exited in-seat banking entirely in 2017 to launch an independent consulting practice — each transition carries asymmetric personal and commercial risk rather than incremental safety.

pace_preference.evidence: His highest-energy operational period was at Sberbank CIB (2014–2017) building a FinTech platform from inception to production inside a mid-sized CIB — a scale-up context rather than a startup greenfield or a mature enterprise steady-state; his ESP practice also serves growth-phase enterprise clients rather than turnaround incumbents.

leadership_style.evidence: Breygin's career shows a consistent pattern of holding singular accountability titles — CIO, COO, Global Head, Practice Director — rather than collaborative peer roles; at Sberbank CIB he owned a $50M P&L and drove Agile transformation top-down, and at ESP he directs 15+ concurrent enterprise programmes as sole practice lead.

psychology.narrative_summary: Breygin is a transformation-first executive who gravitates toward building or overhauling systems rather than running them at steady state, and whose seven-year consulting arc at ESP suggests he now operates best with autonomous scope and diverse mandates rather than inside a single corporate hierarchy — on the job at RBC Capital Markets, a recruiter should expect strong programme design rigour and capital markets stakeholder credibility, but should anticipate friction with the run-the-bank accountability and 24/7 operational governance that a Head of IT Operations role demands. The absence of evidenced headcount scale (no team sizes disclosed for any role) and the consulting-to-operator gap are the two facts a hiring manager will press hardest, and the honest positioning is transformation-first with a complementary operational deputy rather than a full-spectrum IT operations incumbent.
psychology.adversity_response: The most visible inflection point is Breygin's 2017 exit from in-seat banking into independent consulting at ESP; rather than seeking another operator role after Sberbank CIB, he pivoted to an advisory model — a pattern that suggests he responds to institutional constraints by seeking greater autonomy rather than absorbing them, which could signal difficulty re-integrating into a structured corporate hierarchy after seven years of self-directed practice.

change_orientation.evidence: The AI evaluation identifies three substantive transformation programmes: a FinTech trading platform built from inception to production at Sberbank CIB, a global regulatory and risk overhaul at BofA Merrill Lynch, and enterprise-wide digital transformation across 15+ client solutions at ESP — a career-long pattern of building or overhauling rather than optimising existing systems.

motivation_drivers.evidence: Career choices consistently prioritise transformational mandates over incremental management roles — building a FinTech platform from scratch at Sberbank CIB, overseeing a global regulatory overhaul at BofA Merrill Lynch, and directing enterprise digital transformation at ESP all prioritise programme legacy over positional security.

The self-identification as a CPO archetype and the breadth of domain expertise accumulated — capital markets, regulatory technology, Agile, AI, blockchain, digital payments — points to a pattern of building cross-domain capability rather than deepening within a single function.

The consistent pursuit of CIO, COO, and Global Head titles across organisations of varying size, and the current branding as both CPO and Global Head of Transformation at ESP, signals that positional recognition is a meaningful but secondary motivator relative to the impact and mastery signals.

No explicit compensation signals in the CV; the decision to leave a bulge-bracket seat (BofA Merrill Lynch) for Sberbank CIB and then exit banking entirely for independent consulting suggests financial optimisation was not the primary driver at either junction.

collaboration_style.evidence: At ESP he simultaneously manages 15+ enterprise client engagements, which requires orchestrating distributed delivery teams rather than solo execution; the Sberbank CIB Agile transformation also implies deliberate team-structure design as a delivery mechanism, and board-level engagement is cited across CIB and exchange clearing bodies.

hierarchy_preference.evidence: Breygin has self-selected into an independent consulting practice since 2017 and his current title — Global Practice Director, CPO and Global Head of Transformation — sits outside any conventional corporate reporting line; the voluntary departure from structured tier-1 bank environments after 2017 signals a preference for autonomous, flatter operating models.

profile.fit_summary: Against the highest-weighted dimensions of domain (10) and leadership (9), Breygin offers genuine capital markets and CIB domain exposure but has spent seven years in a consulting/product role rather than running a large-scale internal IT operations function — the 400-person team and $100M opex mandate are materially beyond what his CV evidences; on transformation (8) he shows credible programme delivery but the operational depth and in-seat scale required for Head of IT Operations at RBC Capital Markets are not sufficiently demonstrated.

emails.body:
I wanted to introduce Vladimir Breygin as a candidate for the Head of IT Operations role at RBC Capital Markets. I am presenting him with transparency about where he is strong and where the fit requires a structural conversation, because I think the domain question — the dimension your CIO has flagged as non-negotiable — is genuinely answered by his background.

Breygin held a Global Head of Risk & Regulatory seat at Bank of America Merrill Lynch from 2012 to 2014, leading front-to-back delivery of global regulatory and risk programmes at a point of peak post-crisis regulatory pressure. He followed that with a CIO/COO mandate at Sberbank CIB from 2014 to 2017, where he managed a $50M P&L and built a FinTech trading platform from inception to full production. These are not adjacent-fintech or wealth-management backgrounds — they are in-seat capital markets and investment banking roles with direct trading-desk and regulatory accountability.

The two gaps I want to name upfront: his CV does not state headcount for any role, and the $50M Sberbank P&L falls short of the $100M opex threshold the role requires. He has also been operating as an external consultant and Global Practice Director at Enterprise Solution Providers since 2017, directing over 15 enterprise transformation programmes rather than running a large internal IT function. The consulting-to-operator transition is real and should be tested explicitly.

My recommendation is a first-round conversation scoped around the modernisation mandate and domain depth, with headcount and infrastructure scale as the explicit qualification questions. I am happy to brief you in more detail before that call if useful.
emails.subject: Vladimir Breygin — CIB Domain Depth for RBC Head of IT Ops

emails.body:
Following your review of Vladimir Breygin's dossier, I want to get ahead of the two questions I expect are front of mind: leadership scale and post-trade platform ownership.

On scale, the honest position is that his CV does not state team sizes for any role, and the largest budget evidenced is a $50M P&L at Sberbank CIB. Our evaluation model caps his leadership dimension at 6/10 as a result — I have not papered over that. What the CV does evidence is managers-of-managers behaviour through title and programme scope: at Sberbank CIB he owned a P&L and drove Agile transformation across a cross-functional fintech build; at BofA Merrill Lynch he held global programme accountability across a tier-1 investment bank. The right question for a first interview is not whether his current CV number matches the 400-person threshold, but whether his operational pattern scales — and I believe a direct conversation will surface headcount data that the CV omits.

On post-trade platform ownership, the CV is silent on named systems such as Murex, Calypso, or Broadridge. This is a genuine gap against the technical dimension and I have flagged it as such. His BofA Merrill Lynch role sits squarely inside the post-crisis regulatory infrastructure build, which in a tier-1 CIB in that period almost certainly involved at least one major post-trade or risk platform programme — but I cannot assert ownership without named evidence, and that is a direct interview question.

The new angle I would add at this stage is the transformation programme at Sberbank CIB specifically: a FinTech trading platform built from inception to production inside a CIB, with a $50M P&L and reported 40% revenue uplift, is a closer analogue to the modernisation mandate inside the RBC Capital Markets role than most operator-profile candidates in this market can offer. That is the ceiling argument for moving him forward despite the scale gap.
emails.subject: Vladimir Breygin — Addressing Your Scale and Platform Questions

emails.body:
Given the positive HM feedback signals and the productive first-round conversation, I would like to propose a structured second-round panel to qualify the two remaining open questions: operational scale and post-trade platform depth.

My recommendation is a two-part interview. The first part should be a 45-minute session with the Line of Business CIO and the CM COO, focused on the modernisation mandate — specifically how Breygin would structure the simplification programme, what governance model he would apply, and how he would manage the regulatory reporting technology agenda. This is where his BofA Merrill Lynch and Sberbank CIB credentials will be most visible and where the domain depth argument is strongest.

The second part should be a 30-minute technical deep-dive with your Head of Infrastructure or a senior architect, with explicit questions on post-trade platform ownership — ask him directly whether he has held roadmap or vendor-relationship accountability for any of the major clearing or settlement platforms, and probe the Sberbank CIB build for the infrastructure stack he owned. If he cannot name platforms at that session, the technical gap is confirmed and the structural mitigation — appointing a strong Head of Infrastructure as operational deputy — should be tabled as the path forward.

I would suggest scheduling within the next ten days given the timeline concern flagged in feedback. I can coordinate directly with Breygin and provide a structured briefing note for each panel member in advance of the session.

intelligence_report.ai_agenda:
RBC Capital Markets has one of the most concrete and publicly documented AI agendas among global investment banks. The Aiden platform ecosystem — built with RBC Borealis on Nvidia AI Enterprise — is the flagship, encompassing electronic trading (VWAP and Arrival Price deep reinforcement learning algorithms), research acceleration (AidenResearch, QuickTakes built on Databricks), and banker productivity (AidenBanker). As of a March 2026 PYMNTS report, more than 8,000 capital markets employees are already using the Aiden platform. RBC Borealis has filed more than 635 AI-related patents since 2019 and the ATOM foundation model was used across 15 products and processes in 2025. RBC partnered with Cohere in 2025 to develop secure generative AI solutions for financial services, and with Nvidia for customised generative AI deployment. RBC's 2025 Investor Day set a target of $700M–$1B in pre-tax earnings from AI-driven initiatives by 2027, and the firm ranks first in Canada and third globally in the 2025 Evident AI Index.

intelligence_report.executive_summary:
RBC Capital Markets is operating from a position of deliberate technology investment and transformation, with the Capital Markets division explicitly identified as a growth engine within Royal Bank of Canada's broader enterprise strategy. The firm operates 55 offices across 16 countries and, as of February 2026, employs approximately 11,000 people with estimated annual revenues of $15 billion. The CM Tech function is structured around a Line of Business CIO model — the hiring stakeholder is Vlad Breygin, Capital Markets CIO — with a standing CM Tech Operating Committee that the incoming Global Head of CM Operations, Regulatory, and Supervisory Technology will join. The mandate is unambiguous: the role owns all application development for post-execution trade processing (back office) and regulatory/supervisory reporting technology, carries a ~$100MM annual budget and ~400 headcount, and is chartered to drive a major simplification and modernisation initiative across the estate for scale and resilience.

The firm's public posture is biased toward in-house build: the Aiden algorithmic trading platform (built with RBC Borealis using deep reinforcement learning), the Lumina enterprise data and AI platform, the ATOM proprietary foundation model, and the AidenResearch/AidenBanker product suite are all internally developed. In May 2025, RBC Capital Markets formalised a dedicated AI and Digital Innovation team under Lindsay Patrick (Chief Strategy and Innovation Officer) and Bobby Grubert (Head of AI and Digital Innovation). RBC's 2025 Investor Day cited $700M–$1B in pre-tax earnings targeted by 2027 from AI-driven initiatives, and the firm ranked first in Canada and third globally in the 2025 Evident AI Index. The technology posture for back-office and regulatory technology, while less publicly profiled than the front-office AI story, sits squarely in the mandate of this hire — the incumbent will need to translate the firm's front-office innovation ambition into the resilience and simplification of the post-trade and regulatory reporting estate, interfacing daily with the CM COO and her management team.
intelligence_report.technology_strategy:
RBC Capital Markets operates a strongly in-house build posture for strategic technology. Confirmed proprietary platforms include Aiden (deep reinforcement learning electronic trading, launched globally 2020), Lumina (enterprise data and AI platform), ATOM (foundation model for financial services built by RBC Borealis with 100+ researchers, deployed across 15 products and processes in 2025), AidenResearch (AI agents for earnings content, call summarisation, and filing access), AidenBanker (pitchbook and meeting-prep automation), and QuickTakes (research turnaround platform built on Databricks). The disclosed tech stack includes Microsoft, Java, C#, Power BI, and SQL Server. For the post-trade and regulatory estate, the firm's stated goal — sourced from the recruiter brief — is simplification and modernisation for scale and resilience, signalling that the current estate carries legacy complexity typical of a mid-tier global investment bank that has grown through product and geographic expansion. Project Samara (Canada's first blockchain-based bond issuance, settled via distributed ledger in partnership with the Bank of Canada and RBC Investor Services) signals an appetite for post-trade infrastructure experimentation. RBC Clear, a purpose-built digital-first cash management platform launched in 2024–25, won the 2025 Model Bank award for Reinventing Cash Management, reflecting the firm's willingness to decommission legacy workflows and build from scratch when the business case is clear.

The CM technology organisation is governed through a Line of Business CIO model with a standing CM Tech Operating Committee, which the incoming head will join as a standing member. This governance structure implies a reasonably mature technology operating model with cross-functional accountability — budget holders sit alongside the business COO and CIO, not below them. The $100MM annual technology budget for the Operations, Regulatory, and Supervisory Technology tower is material and indicates the firm is prepared to fund the modernisation programme at scale, not incrementally.
intelligence_report.ideal_candidate_profile:
The target archetype is a senior technology executive who has owned — not just contributed to — the post-execution application development estate at a global investment bank or large broker-dealer, with credible capital markets domain depth across equities, fixed income, or multi-asset post-trade. The role carries a $100MM annual budget and ~400 headcount, so the candidate must have demonstrated managers-of-managers leadership at comparable scale; direct headcount and budget ownership must be named and verifiable, not inferred. The standing membership on the CM Tech Operating Committee and the daily interface with the CM COO require executive maturity: the ability to translate complex technology states into business risk language for non-technical COO-level stakeholders, and to hold ground on architectural decisions under commercial pressure. Given the firm's confirmed in-house build posture and proprietary platform investments, candidates from pure third-party system integrator or outsourced operations backgrounds will likely struggle to earn credibility with the engineering-heavy RBC Borealis-influenced technology culture.

On transformation, the mandate explicitly requires driving a simplification and modernisation initiative — the Post-Trade Systems Check skill applies in full here. Candidates must be able to name at least one analogous programme with budget, duration, platforms decommissioned or migrated, and measurable outcome (e.g. settlement fail-rate improvement, regulatory submission latency reduction, system consolidation from N to M). Regulatory exposure is non-negotiable: the role owns supervisory and regulatory reporting technology, so familiarity with SEC Rule 15c3-3, CAT, Reg SCI, and/or EMIR/MiFID II reporting infrastructure (depending on geography) must be demonstrable by named programme, not generic compliance language. Candidates who have navigated a T+1 readiness programme, a regulatory remediation driven by SEC/FINRA/FCA findings, or a CCP/clearing-house integration bring concrete differentiation that maps directly to the stated scope.

The right question for a first interview is not whether his current CV number matches the 400-person threshold, but whether his operational pattern scales — and I believe a direct conversation will surface headcount data that the CV omits.

On post-trade platform ownership, the CV is silent on named systems such as Murex, Calypso, or Broadridge. This is a genuine gap against the technical dimension and I have flagged it as such. His BofA Merrill Lynch role sits squarely inside the post-crisis regulatory infrastructure build, which in a tier-1 CIB in that period almost certainly involved at least one major post-trade or risk platform programme — but I cannot assert ownership without named evidence, and that is a direct interview question.

The new angle I would add at this stage is the transformation programme at Sberbank CIB specifically: a FinTech trading platform built from inception to production inside a CIB, with a $50M P&L and reported 40% revenue uplift, is a closer analogue to the modernisation mandate inside the RBC Capital Markets role than most operator-profile candidates in this market can offer. That is the ceiling argument for moving him forward despite the scale gap.
emails.subject: Vladimir Breygin — Addressing Your Scale and Platform Questions

emails.body:
Given the positive HM feedback signals and the productive first-round conversation, I would like to propose a structured second-round panel to qualify the two remaining open questions: operational scale and post-trade platform depth.

My recommendation is a two-part interview. The first part should be a 45-minute session with the Line of Business CIO and the CM COO, focused on the modernisation mandate — specifically how Breygin would structure the simplification programme, what governance model he would apply, and how he would manage the regulatory reporting technology agenda. This is where his BofA Merrill Lynch and Sberbank CIB credentials will be most visible and where the domain depth argument is strongest.

The second part should be a 30-minute technical deep-dive with your Head of Infrastructure or a senior architect, with explicit questions on post-trade platform ownership — ask him directly whether he has held roadmap or vendor-relationship accountability for any of the major clearing or settlement platforms, and probe the Sberbank CIB build for the infrastructure stack he owned. If he cannot name platforms at that session, the technical gap is confirmed and the structural mitigation — appointing a strong Head of Infrastructure as operational deputy — should be tabled as the path forward.

I would suggest scheduling within the next ten days given the timeline concern flagged in feedback. I can coordinate directly with Breygin and provide a structured briefing note for each panel member in advance of the session.
